items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: And Joe and Sonny were two of the most colorful characters in the band, which was full of colorful characters.

ctx.x: I have that album with the arrangements right on the “Basie Swings” and the —

Yeah and “Joe Williams Sings Basie Swings” yes, yes, that was— Thad Jones also did some wonderful work for Joe, as well as Ernie Wilkins. Ernie Wilkins, he wrote the big, the arrangement on the big hit “Every Day” and there was another one called “Five O’clock in the Morning.”

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...plus with Joe Williams on board... [INTERVIEWEE] Yes. It definitely is documented... That is Count Basie, the New Testament Count Basie.

ctx.x: Eleven years, wow. And you had mentioned Sinatra, and thinking about vocalists, did the guys in the band ever kind of resent the vocalist being out front and doing four or five songs a night and was that something that you guys felt like you didn’t feel it was necessary?

Well the professionalism in this particular orchestra didn’t allow for that kind of attitude on a large scale. And we loved Sinatra, we loved Billy Eckstine, we loved Sarah Vaughan and we loved Tony Bennett, and there just was no feeling of that kind. Whenever we knew we were going to work with them we said well we’re going to have some fun now. Some others, who shall remain nameless, we didn’t have as much fun with because some of them didn’t have the quality arrangements that we would like to play, and some of…
Well you certainly had a powerhouse band there for those years, plus with Joe Williams on board, and a great time. Fortunately you recorded a lot so it’s documented. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

items.title: Joe Williams interviewed by Leslie Gourse, New York City, New York, March 9, 1996
items.q: Frank Foster and Ernie Wilkins, we got together... They made the arrangements on 'Every Day I Have the Blues'... 'The Comeback' and 'Every Day I’ve Fallen in Love All Over Again With You' that Foster did for me

ctx.x: Harry “Sweets” Edison, and I like that Bohanon, the trombonist you worked with, and so many of them. I mean I love them. Jimmy Jones and everyone.
Yup, yup, yup, yup, yup. Hank Jones, Jimmy Jones, Osie Johnson, Milt Hinton, Kenny Burrell, oh boy, Romeo Penque, Harold Lookofsky. Really all these wonderful — Zoot Sims, Frank Foster, and —
And the Jones-Lewis band. The Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band.

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Writing for Joe was pretty much a snap... I was happy to be the arranger of the Comeback... Joe Williams says, 'When the train rolls up.'

ctx.x: Do you think this was a feeling held by others in the band at that time?

Possibly so. There was a trumpeter named Don Rader who quit the same night I did. He probably had the same reasons, because he had a family of youngsters. He had two very young children, and he might have wanted to play more. You play a whole set, like an hour set, and you play maybe one or two solos. You go home and you say, “What have I done tonight?” And then a lot of arrangements from other arrangers were coming in to the band that I didn’t consider that all that -- all of that. Joe Williams was singing, and…
Talk a bit about writing for Joe [Williams], your contributions in that area and what particular challenge that might have been or what approach you felt he needed.
